prior_inspection.title: Alexander Wolitzky, MIT 14.121: Lectures 1–2, Choice, Preference, and Utility (2015)
prior_inspection.use: Method reference for complete/transitive preferences, ordinal representations, continuity, monotonicity/local nonsatiation, convex/strictly convex preferences and quasiconcavity; complete-choice-correspondence WARP convention.
prior_inspection.verification: Retrieved the actual 33-page official MIT lecture PDF and inspected numbered slides7–16 and20–27, including the formal correspondence WARP definition on slide11, strictly increasing representation rule, finite versus infinite representation distinction, LNS and the upper-contour/quasiconcavity statements. Used only these stable method passages. The chapter supplies original definitions/examples and proofs, does not copy source exercises or assert the source's wider rationalization/representation theorems without their full hypotheses, and does not rely on the later separability section.

selected_scope.topic: Choice data, nonempty feasible correspondences, complete/transitive preferences, exact maximal-set rationalization, direct weak/strict revelation, correspondence WARP and the all-pairs/all-triples theorem.
Ordinal representation, strictly increasing transformations, finite weak orders, lexicographic nonrepresentability, sequential closed-graph continuity and a representation existence statement.
Regularity definitions and distinctions: weak/strict coordinate monotonicity, local nonsatiation, convex/strictly convex preferences, convex maximal sets, and quasiconcavity rather than concavity.

theorem_hypotheses: A choice domain consists of nonempty menus B subset X, with a nonempty C(B) subset B. The source rationalization uses equality with the full set of maximal alternatives, not merely inclusion of a selected observation among possibly many maxima.

The WARP sufficiency/uniqueness statement on slide 13 assumes that the menu domain contains every nonempty subset of X with at most three elements. The preference is complete and transitive. All menus in the specified domain, not only pairs, must be rationalized.
Finite utility representation requires a complete transitive relation on the finite alternative set. An arbitrary real-valued representation implies those order properties.
Slide 16 uses the full uncountable square [0,1]^2 with lexicographic priority. It asserts no real-valued representation at all, a stronger statement than failure of a continuous representation.

Slide 17 assumes X subset R^n with its relative Euclidean topology and closed graph of the weak relation, stated through simultaneous convergent sequences, together with rationality. It states existence of a utility representation but provides no proof or explicit continuous-utility conclusion.

Monotonicity and strict monotonicity in slides 20-22 use x>=y coordinatewise, and strictness when at least one coordinate is greater. Local nonsatiation is a separate relative-domain neighborhood property. Convexity claims require the relevant mixtures to belong to the consumption domain.
transcription_and_scope_cautions: The text extractor renders the weak preference symbol as t and sometimes loses the nonmembership stroke in WARP. The actual images of slides 11 and 13 confirm the quantifiers and nonmembership condition.

The short summary on slide 18 does not repeat the menu-richness assumption. The eventual chapter must carry the full slide-13 hypothesis, not repeat the summary as a theorem on arbitrary observed menus.

The slide-17 result must not be described as a supplied constructive proof of a continuous utility representation. The proposed orthant/strict-monotonicity route below is an original sufficient construction with stronger stated assumptions.
Convex preferences imply quasiconcavity of a representing utility. Concavity of a particular ordinal representation is a stronger property and is not invariant under every increasing transformation.
The lecture theorem statements are source support, not evidence that the planned chapter has already supplied their proofs. Separability on slides 29-32 was excluded.

sources.title: Hal R. Varian, The Nonparametric Approach to Demand Analysis, Econometrica 50(4), 945-973 (July 1982)
sources.publication_version: Original 1982 journal article reproduced in a public university-hosted PDF. The JSTOR cover identifies July 1982, volume 50, number 4 and pages 945-973. The PDF creation date 27 February 2008 is an archive-generation date, not publication. The 2014 URL path and 2016 HTTP last-modified are host provenance, not article versions.
sources.mapping: Physical page 1 is the JSTOR bibliographic/copyright cover. Physical pages 2-30 correspond to printed journal pages 945-973 by printed=physical+943. Physical pages 31-34 are later linked-citation pages, not the original article body.
sources.navigation_only: Page headings from the complete extraction were inspected only to locate Appendix I. No empirical applications, welfare recovery/extrapolation results or later linked citations are claimed read.

selected_scope.topic: Finite observed budgets; rationalization as optimality of each selected bundle; trivial constant-utility warning; cyclical consistency/GARP and SARP distinctions; transitive-closure test and the beginning of the recoverability motivation.

Appendix I: finite reflexive/transitive maximal-element procedure, constructive Afriat numbers, the three induction cases, local-nonsatiation necessity, lower-envelope utility and budget optimality. Page 970 also contains an explicitly heuristic differentiable interpretation and the heading/introduction of Appendix II.

theorem_hypotheses: Use an explicitly finite dataset indexed t=1,...,T, finite L>=1, observed nonnegative bundles x^t in R_+^L and strictly positive finite price vectors p^t in R_++^L. The selected bundle spends the modeled income m_t=p^t dot x^t, so the complete budget is {x>=0:p^t dot x<=m_t}. These domain/sign conditions must be made explicit in the eventual chapter; the inspected article uses economic price/quantity notation without restating every sign condition at each theorem.
Rationalization means x^t belongs to the maximizing set at its observed budget. It does not assert that the selected observation records all maximizers or that choices are unique.

For necessity, the actual proof on printed page 969 invokes local nonsatiation on the nonnegative consumption domain. The theorem shortens this to nonsatiated; global absence of a global best point is not the local premise used by that proof.

Define direct weak revelation by p^t dot x^t >= p^t dot x^s and take its reflexive transitive closure R. GARP requires p^s dot x^s <= p^s dot x^t whenever t R s. Equality is allowed. This is equivalent to excluding a directed affordability cycle with at least one strict edge.

The Afriat system is U_s <= U_t+lambda_t*p^t dot (x^s-x^t) for every ordered pair, with real U_t and strictly positive lambda_t. A common additive shift makes all finite U_t positive if desired. Positivity of the multipliers cannot be relaxed to allowing them all to be zero.

Under the explicit strictly positive prices, the constructed lower envelope is continuous, concave and strictly increasing in the coordinatewise order, and therefore locally nonsatiated. The proof requires no differentiability and permits tied observations and nonsmooth utility.
transcription_and_scope_cautions: The extraction confuses lambda with X and the weak inequalities with digits, and can reverse superscripts. Images of printed pages 946-947 and 968-970 were inspected to fix the actual quantifiers and indices.

Printed page 970 first displayed evaluation of U(x^i) uses the reversed difference x^m-x^i in the affine term. The envelope defined on page 969 instead evaluates U_m+lambda_m*p^m dot (x^i-x^m). Avoid copying the problematic line: the Afriat inequalities give each affine term at x^i at least U_i, while the self-index term equals U_i, proving equality directly.

Printed page 968 Algorithm 3 has step-5 denominator p^i dot (x^j-x^i), not the reverse. Its positivity requires the previously selected classes and maximality argument; it is not a generic assumption that all cross-expenditure differences are positive.

The source theorem says nonsatiated, but its necessity argument explicitly uses local nonsatiation to improve a strictly interior affordable comparison. Preserve the local condition instead of weakening it through shorthand.

The page-946 informal description of a nonnegative linear system must not be implemented with only lambda>=0: the all-zero solution would accept arbitrary data. Strict multipliers can be normalized to lambda_t>=1 by a common positive rescaling in a finite dataset; utility levels remain freely shiftable.

The differentiable heuristic on page 970 writes Du(x^j)=lambda_j*p^j. On R_+^L this needs interior choices or suitable additional conditions; at a corner there are nonnegativity multipliers. The actual finite Afriat construction does not require or use this heuristic.

Passing GARP establishes existence of a regular rationalizer under these budgets. It neither identifies the true utility nor establishes that all observationally equivalent true preferences are concave. The source SARP discussion must not be interpreted as proving empirical global uniqueness of an unobserved demand correspondence.

proof_requirements_and_routes.topic: Finite weak-order representation and ordinal uniqueness
proof_requirements_and_routes.status: Elementary route for future authoring; not a completed chapter proof
proof_requirements_and_routes.hypotheses: Finite nonempty X; complete transitive weak preference.
proof_requirements_and_routes.route: Prove that indifference is an equivalence relation and that the induced order on its classes is a complete strict order. Rank the finitely many classes and assign those ranks to their members. This gives x weakly preferred to y exactly when u(x)>=u(y). Conversely a real-valued representation inherits completeness/transitivity. If v is another representation, equal u-values imply indifference and equal v-values, so define a strictly increasing transformation on the range u(X).
proof_requirements_and_routes.prerequisites_to_supply: Equivalence classes and a finite ordered-class enumeration; distinguish ordinal certain-choice utility from the positive-affine restriction for expected utility over lotteries.

proof_requirements_and_routes.topic: Lexicographic failure of every real-valued representation
proof_requirements_and_routes.status: Elementary contradiction route; stronger than the existing V05 continuous-representation counterexample
proof_requirements_and_routes.hypotheses: Lexicographic order on the full [0,1]^2, with first coordinate strictly prioritized.
proof_requirements_and_routes.route: If u represented it, for each t the interval (u(t,0),u(t,1)) would be nonempty. For t<s, lexicographic order gives u(t,1)<u(s,0), so these intervals are pairwise disjoint. Choose the first rational in each interval under a fixed enumeration of Q. This injects uncountably many t into Q, a contradiction. The argument rules out any real-valued representation, not just continuous ones.
proof_requirements_and_routes.prerequisites_to_supply: Density and countability of Q, uncountability of [0,1], and the explicit first-rational rule. If these facts have not been proved in prerequisites, supply their short countability/diagonal arguments.

proof_requirements_and_routes.topic: A fully elementary sufficient continuous representation on the consumption orthant
proof_requirements_and_routes.status: Root approved this bounded sufficient route on 9 October 2026; final theorem contract remains root-owned
proof_requirements_and_routes.hypotheses: X=R_+^L for finite L>=1; the preference is complete and transitive; its weak graph is closed under simultaneous convergent sequences in X; it is strictly coordinate-monotone: x>=y and x!=y imply x strictly preferred to y.
proof_requirements_and_routes.route: For each x, 0 is weakly below x and M times the all-ones vector is weakly above x when M>=max_i x_i. Along the diagonal, closed weak upper/lower cuts cover [0,M] and are both nonempty; interval connectedness (or a proved infimum argument) gives an indifferent diagonal t*1. Strict monotonicity makes this t unique. Let u(x)=t. Transitivity and the diagonal order establish exact representation. If x_n->x, the associated t_n are bounded by max_i x_ni. Every convergent subsequence of t_n has limit t with t*1 indifferent to x by closed graph, hence t=u(x). Boundedness and subsequence uniqueness give t_n->u(x), proving continuity.
proof_requirements_and_routes.prerequisites_to_supply: Connected intervals or an explicit cut/infimum proof; compact subsequence theorem; treatment of x=0; definition of relative-domain continuity. No convexity of preferences or differentiability is required.
proof_requirements_and_routes.general_scope_not_claimed: This does not prove the general continuous-representation theorem on every Euclidean subset without monotonicity or a diagonal path. MIT slide 17 states representation existence without proving the broader construction. Root must either retain the sufficient orthant theorem or separately supply the broader proof and its topological hypotheses.

proof_requirements_and_routes.topic: Correspondence WARP on a sufficiently rich menu domain
proof_requirements_and_routes.hypotheses: A nonempty C(B) subset B for every B in the menu family; every singleton, pair and triple belongs to that family. Rationalization means equality with all weak maxima.
proof_requirements_and_routes.route: Use pair choices to define x R y iff x is chosen from {x,y}; nonemptiness gives completeness. WARP equates this pair relation with weak revelation from arbitrary observed menus. To prove transitivity, if x R y and y R z but not x R z, nonempty choice on {x,y,z} and successive WARP implications force choices incompatible with the pair {x,z}. For an observed menu, every chosen x is above every available y. Conversely if x is above every menu alternative, choose any z from the nonempty observed C(B); pairwise x R z and WARP imply x is also chosen. Pair choices uniquely determine the rationalizing weak order.
proof_requirements_and_routes.prerequisites_to_supply: Handle ties and repeated alternatives explicitly. WARP necessity under a fixed weak order holds on any menu domain, but this sufficiency proof uses the triple domain. Do not infer existence of a maximum on arbitrary infinite menus from rationality alone.

proof_requirements_and_routes.topic: Restricted finite menus and equality versus selected-choice rationalization
proof_requirements_and_routes.status: Potential elementary completion criterion; final chapter design not prescribed
proof_requirements_and_routes.hypotheses: Finite X and a finite family of nonempty menus with nonempty complete reported choice sets.
proof_requirements_and_routes.route: Record weak edges from each chosen alternative to every available alternative, marking the edges to excluded alternatives strict. A weak-order exact rationalizer cannot have a directed cycle containing a strict edge. Conversely, if no such cycle exists, collapse mutually reachable weak-edge classes and assign ordered ranks along a topological ordering of the finite acyclic quotient. No strict edge is internal to a class. The resulting utility makes all and only the reported choices maximize each observed menu.
proof_requirements_and_routes.prerequisites_to_supply: Prove finite directed reachability classes and existence of an acyclic ordering, rather than invoking an unproved graph algorithm. This is different from treating a single observed budget choice as the complete maximizing set. Pairwise WARP alone on a restricted menu family need not rule out a longer cycle.

proof_requirements_and_routes.status: Original inequality proof route supported by Varian pages 946-949 and969
proof_requirements_and_routes.hypotheses: Finite positive-price, nonnegative-bundle dataset with complete linear budgets and observed expenditure equal to income; utility rationalization with local nonsatiation.
proof_requirements_and_routes.route: An affordable observation implies a weak utility comparison. If it is strictly cheaper, local nonsatiation supplies a nearby strictly better bundle still inside the same budget, so equality in utility would contradict maximization; this gives a strict utility comparison. Chain weak comparisons through the transitive closure. A strictly affordable reverse comparison would create a strict utility cycle, giving GARP. Conversely a GARP violation supplies a concrete cycle with a strict edge, and every such cycle violates GARP.
proof_requirements_and_routes.prerequisites_to_supply: The strict slack must leave a relative-domain neighborhood inside the budget. Keep tie-permitting budget WARP, longer GARP chains, SARP and full-correspondence WARP as separately displayed conditions.

proof_requirements_and_routes.topic: Constructive Afriat feasibility without an unproved linear-programming oracle
proof_requirements_and_routes.status: Finite induction route checked against the actual Appendix I text and equation images
proof_requirements_and_routes.hypotheses: The same finite dataset satisfies GARP; use the reflexive transitive revealed relation R.
proof_requirements_and_routes.route: Among the remaining indices choose an R-maximal class E (no remaining strictly higher predecessor) and remove classes in that order; let B be previously assigned indices. At the first class take common U and lambda positive. For a later class choose U_E as the minimum of U_j and U_j+lambda_j*p^j dot (x^i-x^j) over i in E,j in B. For each such pair p^i dot (x^j-x^i)>0, since otherwise i R j and i would have been assigned no later than j. Choose a common lambda_E at least one and at least every (U_j-U_E)/(p^i dot (x^j-x^i)). This supplies inequalities in both directions between the new and old classes. Inside E the utilities are equal and GARP gives the required nonnegative cross-expenditure terms. Induct until every index is assigned. A finite common additive shift adjusts the utility levels if positive labels are desired.
proof_requirements_and_routes.prerequisites_to_supply: Prove finite maximal-class existence and termination, each denominator sign, all three induction cases, and positivity of multipliers. Do not merely quote Algorithm 3 or claim an unexecuted LP proves feasibility.

proof_requirements_and_routes.topic: Afriat lower envelope and all required shape/optimality properties
proof_requirements_and_routes.status: Direct finite-affine proof route with the source display correction made explicit
proof_requirements_and_routes.hypotheses: U_s <= U_t+lambda_t*p^t dot (x^s-x^t) for every pair; lambda_t>0 and p^t in R_++^L.
proof_requirements_and_routes.route: Define u(x) as the minimum over t of U_t+lambda_t*p^t dot (x-x^t). Finitely many affine terms give continuity, and taking the minimum preserves concavity by the defining concavity inequality. For x>=y,x!=y, every affine difference is positive, with a positive minimum over the finite index set; hence u(x)>u(y), implying local nonsatiation. At an observed x^s, every term is at least U_s by the Afriat inequalities and its own term equals U_s, so u(x^s)=U_s. If x is affordable at budget s, its s-term is at most U_s, hence u(x)<=U_s. This proves rationalization without derivative or interior assumptions.
proof_requirements_and_routes.prerequisites_to_supply: Do not reverse the vector difference in the source page-970 first display. Do not claim differentiability or unique demand from a minimum of affine functions. Strictly positive prices support the strict coordinate-monotonicity conclusion.

proof_requirements_and_routes.status: Implementation requirements only; no chapter lab or prototype produced
proof_requirements_and_routes.hypotheses: Exact finite declared dataset; explicit numeric representation and inequality convention.
proof_requirements_and_routes.route: Compute direct affordability edges and their transitive closure, retaining a path for any strict reversal. A future bounded standard-library checker can verify every candidate Afriat inequality and the lower-envelope certificate independently. If presenting linear feasibility, use lambda_t>=1 after a justified common positive rescaling; allowing all-zero multipliers is invalid. Any tolerance for measured data must be a separately defined perturbed test, not silent strict-to-weak inequality changes.
proof_requirements_and_routes.prerequisites_to_supply: Supply the finite reachability proof or a transparent path enumeration at the chosen bounded size. GARP success is a model-existence statement conditional on fixed preferences, observed prices/bundles and complete budgets; it is not identification of the true utility, a test of every omitted constraint, or a statistical confidence statement.
